During the time set aside for matters on the agenda but not listed for public hearing, individuals may address the Board of Supervisors concerning matters previously considered by the board or matters that are pending before the board other than items listed on the agenda for public hearing. Individuals are allowed one opportunity of up to three minutes to speak at each board meeting during matters from the public.

The sign-up sheet is managed by the clerk's office. Timekeeping is conducted through a timer and light system at the podium. The green light will go on when you begin speaking, which begins your allotted time. The yellow light indicates you have one minute to finish speaking. The red light indicates your time has expired, and you will be asked to end your comments.

To give all speakers equal treatment and courtesy, the board requests that speakers adhere to the following guidelines. When addressing the board, state your name, and if you live in Almar County, your magisterial district. Address comments directly to the board as a whole. Any written statements or other supporting materials may be given to the clerk.

If representing a group or organization, you may ask others to raise their hands in recognition. Speakers may not share any unused time with another speaker. Back and forth debate is not permitted, and please do not speak from your seat or out of turn. All comments are live streamed, recorded, and published on the Almar County website.

My name is Denise Zito. I have been a resident of Free Union for 47 years. That's in the Whitehall Magisterial District. I address you this evening to advocate for an increase in the Albemarle County Emergency Relief Program, the budget that is set up to prevent evictions.

I'm the treasurer of the local conference of the Society of St. Vincent de Paul. This is a worldwide Catholic organization founded 200 years ago, though our local chapter is now four years old. The four Catholic churches in the area contribute the funds, and we distribute over $150,000 every year for housing and utility needs.

We're locally funded, and we support local needs in Charlottesville and Albemarle. We've been focusing our efforts on people facing eviction and utility cutoffs. We recently learned that the eviction rate in the Charlottesville area is the highest in the state due to the high cost of living and the lack of housing.

And the stories that come to us are heartbreaking. Single mothers with children, disabled people, veterans. One unexpected expense throws their budget off balance and they get behind in the rent. Many of the people we serve work for those wonderful subcontractors that UVA employs.

So when the students are on break, the contractor's workers' hours are reduced. They aren't eligible for unemployment, and they get behind in their bills. Often the situation snowballs, and they get further behind, and so they must choose between food and rent.

When someone contacts us for assistance, two of our members visit them in their homes and assess the situation and see how we can help. We also pray with them if they would like, and we help them plan for the future. and then we deliver a check to prevent the eviction.

We only assist an individual or family once a year. We receive far more requests for assistance than we can accommodate. We helped over 400 families last year, and we cannot meet the need of all those who ask for assistance. Until we address our housing crisis, which I understand the board is still considering whether to fund the Affordable Housing Trust Fund, the Board of Supervisors and charitable organizations like ours must continue to assist people to enable them to stay at their homes.

And this is being led by Mr. Andy Herrick, our acting county attorney. Good evening, Mr. Chair, members of the board. Andy Herrick, I'm the interim county attorney. for quite some time. I want to make sure that everyone is kind of up to speed and it'll be a brief summary on this. And, you know, an overview of this is this project is a development of a road network, a new road network at the site of the former Barnes Lumber site in downtown Crozet.

It will eventually connect Crozet Avenue, Library Avenue, and the square to Hilltop Road and Parkside Village. When we complete this, our intention is to have this road network accepted into the VDOT system. So all the design has been done per VDOT standards, approvals, and so forth.

The area marked in red is the Square and Oak Street Improvements Project. That's a separate project, and we are starting construction in just a few weeks on January 6, 2025. We were ready to go this month, but we figured that the merchants there that were working, you know, we didn't want to interrupt their holiday business.

So we're starting right after the holidays. And so that's real exciting news, and we're looking forward to getting that going. The project itself, as a reminder, is a public-private partnership. Funding is being provided by the developer, the county, and VDOT through revenue-sharing grant funding.

The road system and its connections are consistent with the Crozet master plan, In particular, additional street connections and, of course, obviously the successful redevelopment of downtown Crozet, which is a big goal stated in the Crozet master plan.
The project, as a reminder, the total project budget is just over $8 million. Right now, the current phase that we're in is the right-of-way phase. We've agreed on three of the nine parcels.

One of the parcels is what we'll be discussing this evening. And we're also, our design professionals, are working on finishing up the 90% complete plans for our next submission to VDOT. And let me, I meant to say the construction bidding process, right now we're anticipating starting that in June of 2025.

Typically that takes two to three months from start to finish, and the finish being the award of contract. And once we get to that award of contract, there'll be a notice to proceed issued, and then we anticipate construction activities taking about 12 months to complete.
And with that, I will hand this back to Andy to talk about the parcel itself. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you, Blake. So I'll briefly describe the parcel and then the process as well.

As you can see here on the map, the subject parcel is outlined in yellow to the right side of the parcel. It is to the east of the former Barnes Lumberyard and is at the western end of Hilltop Street in the Parkside Village area. It's parcel number 56A2-04-A3.

It's seven one-hundredths of an acre. And again, it's currently an unused stub of the western terminus of Hilltop Street in Parkside Village. It was initially thought to be owned by the Parkside Village Homeowners Association. But through the process of acquiring the property, a title examination was performed, and it's actually owned by Hauser Homes, Inc., which is a defunct Virginia corporation.

The title has transferred by law to the unknown trustees in liquidation of that company, according to the title exam, and the company and therefore the parcel are further subject to multiple judgments. So eminent domain is really the only practical way to acquire clear title, which is needed for the project to proceed.

Our staff and our outside agents have done a fantastic job of working with property owners to try to make voluntary agreements for conveyance. But this is a case in which the title of the property just isn't clear because it's owned by a defunct corporation and subject to many judgments.

Fortunately, the eminent domain process is able to help clear a variety of problems on the parcel. And the process that's needed is staff has prepared and submitted to you a proposed resolution. It's lengthier than many of the resolutions that you see, but it was prepared, again, with the help of outside counsel.

That's attachment B attached to the staff report. And with the assistance of outside counsel, the county would then file a certificate of take with the court and deposit into the court the estimated value of the parcel, which is $900. In so doing, the county would immediately acquire clear title and can proceed with the project, and then it's up to the court to determine the actual value of the parcel and to distribute the proceeds to the appropriate parties.

But again, this is the way that the county can acquire a clear title without a problem. So I have a suggested motion language here to adopt the resolution attached to the staff report as attachment B. And with that, I'm happy to answer any questions that you may have.

Is it possible that after we have deposited the value with the court that we would later have whoever bought the outstanding judgments then come to us and say, well, we now actually think you owe us significantly more than this?

Is that possible, or would that be the court's problem at that point? It would be up to the court to determine the value of the property. What would be at issue in the case would be the fair market value of the property, not the judgment. My suspicion is that the range of value on a 7 100th acre piece of property is pretty limited. the county would not be liable for satisfying any judgments that the current owner has. Again, so the county's liability would be limited to the actual value of the property acquired and not any outstanding judgments against the current owner.

On board, this brings us to our third public hearing, SP-2024-02, Midway-Martin Store Power Line Upgrade. This one is being led by Mr. Kevin McDermott, Deputy Director of Planning. Welcome, Mr. McDermott.

Thank you, Chair Andrews and members of the Board of Supervisors. My name is Kevin McDermott. I'm the Deputy Director of Planning. And tonight I will be doing the presentation of the staff report for SP 2024 to Midway to Martin Store transmission line phase two project.
So this is an application to upgrade approximately 2.8 miles of transmission line from Thunder Ridge Road in southwest Albemarle County to the Martin Store substation in Nelson County.

This is phase two of the project. The first phase stretched from the Thunder Ridge Road northward along Craigstor Road. And I do have my laser pointer up here if you want to follow along. This is Craigstor Road. The red line is the route of the power line.

So the first phase went from Thunder Ridge Road northward up to the Midway Station near the intersection of Midway Road and Miller School Road just off this map. The existing 60 to 70-foot tall wooden H-poles are proposed to be replaced with 58 to 82.5-foot steel monopoles within the existing right-of-way of the power line.

The map shows the transmission line and, of course, it extends down into Nelson County to approximately Route 151 at the Martin Store substation. The upgrade is occurring because the existing wooden poles are approximately 40 years old and are starting to show signs of deterioration.

The line serves approximately 6,750 customers, and the replacement will improve the reliability of the service. So this is requiring a special use permit because when the initial transmission line went in, that was not a requirement.

Now that they're coming in for the upgrade, the special use permit is required under Section 10.2.26 of the zoning ordinance. Approximately 41 parcels are crossed by this right-of-way, and they're shown in blue in this map.

The green just shows the adjacent parcels. The current zoning in the area is rural area, and the comprehensive plan of future land use is also rural area. The analysis of special use permit requests has us analyze the project against a certain number of factors.

The first of those is that there will be no substantial detriment to adjacent lots. The proposal is for replacement of the existing poles within the existing right-of-way.
